title: Characteristics of Radio
summary: Audience: the group of people whom radio reaches for a programme. Listener: a person or group forming the target audience. Broadcaster: a person who presents or announces programmes over radio. Broadcasting: any communication or transmission of a message or signal to the public through electronic apparatus. Tuning into radio: switching on the radio and selecting the station. Live broadcast: a programme broadcast directly without pre-recording. Pre-recorded programme: recorded on magnetic tape, discs or CDs for later broadcast. Script: the written copy of the words to be spoken in a radio programme. Sanjay in the Mahabharata can be called the first 'radio broadcaster'.

Radio informs (advertisements, water supply announcements, polio immunisation day), educates (agricultural programmes for farmers; Gyanvani, the educational radio station) and entertains (film songs, music, casual comments). For many people radio is the only source of information, education and entertainment; the three objectives are interrelated.

Radio makes pictures (listeners visualise the Republic Day parade commentary using imagination); it is the fastest, instant medium (news a few minutes old, while a newspaper gives the previous day's news); simple technology; inexpensive (a small radio costs about fifty rupees); needs no electric supply (dry battery cells); portable (kitchen, car, travel); needs no literacy (any language can be heard); the only source of news and entertainment for the majority in rural India; the best medium of entertainment with classical, light classical, light, devotional, folk and film music.

A one-chance medium (the spoken word is momentary and cannot be re-read, and you cannot check a dictionary without missing the rest); no visual images (seeing is believing: the cyclone Nargis on television is more effective); messages are easily forgotten; poor performance by announcers makes listeners switch off; no use to people with hearing disabilities.

objective: State true or false: (i) Radio is a slow medium. (ii) One has to be literate to listen to radio.
Fill in the blanks: The three objectives of radio are to ______, ______ and ______.
Match: (i) Broadcaster (ii) Script (iii) Live broadcast (iv) Pre-recorded programme with (a) no pre-recording (b) written words to be spoken (c) recorded for later (d) presents programmes.
State true or false: (i) Radio messages are easily forgotten. (ii) Radio gives visual images.
vsa: What is meant by 'radio is a one-chance medium'?
A listener gets only one chance to hear and understand the spoken message, which cannot be re-read like print.
Name any two characteristics of radio.
It makes pictures in the mind; it is fast, simple, inexpensive and portable.
Any communication or transmission of a message or signal to the public through electronic apparatus.
Why is radio useful in rural areas?
It is cheap, battery run, needs no literacy and is the only source of news and entertainment for the rural majority.
sa: Briefly discuss any three limitations of radio broadcast.
It is a one-chance medium as the spoken word is momentary; it has no visual images so is less convincing than television; and messages are easily forgotten.
Describe the objectives of radio with examples.
To inform (water supply announcements), to educate (agriculture programmes, Gyanvani) and to entertain (film songs).
Explain why radio is called a medium that 'makes pictures'.
Listeners visualise scenes from sound, e.g. commentary on the Republic Day parade, using imagination.
la: Radio as a medium has certain characteristic features. Explain.
It makes pictures, is the fastest and simplest medium, inexpensive, runs on batteries, is portable, needs no literacy and serves the rural majority with music and news.
Explain in detail the limitations of radio.
One-chance medium, no visuals, messages easily forgotten, poor announcers lose listeners, and no use for people with hearing disabilities.
